PNRR classification: where do the funds go?¶

Executive summary¶

Purpose and scope. This project asks whether short Italian PNRR project titles can help analysts suggest one of eight recorded programme themes. It provides a complete, reproducible research workflow with two neural models, simpler reference models, performance plots, explanations and an export demonstration. The labels come from programme metadata; independent review is needed to establish each project's actual purpose.

What the saved experiment found. Starting with 298,338 project records, cleaning produced 166,521 distinct eligible titles. Training used 24,000 titles, validation used 8,000, and evaluation retained all 21,219 test titles from 24 independent programme groups. Keeping related projects together makes this a demanding test of unfamiliar programmes, while removing repeated titles prevents administrative templates from dominating the score.

Approach Match with recorded theme Score giving every theme equal weight (macro-F1)
Simple logistic classifier 42.1% 0.381
Neural model using word features (MLP) 44.4% 0.389
Neural model using local word patterns (CNN) 41.8% 0.288

Accuracy is the share of titles matching their recorded theme. Macro-F1 balances missed and incorrect suggestions within each theme and then averages across themes; it is not a percentage of correct answers. The MLP was selected using validation results. Its advantage over logistic regression was only 0.008 in macro-F1, with an exploratory uncertainty interval from −0.032 to +0.042. This does not establish dependable neural improvement. The proposed 0.80 score and 0.03 improvement goals were missed; the original hypothesis involving independently reviewed project purposes remains untested.

What explains the decision. Training performance improved much more than performance on unfamiliar titles, indicating overfitting. Category results were uneven: education/research was strongest and digitalisation weakest. Test titles contained more words outside the CNN's training vocabulary than training titles did. Its selected training run took about 5.6 minutes, compared with about 4.3 seconds for the selected MLP; vocabulary shift is a plausible contributor to its lower result, not a proven cause. These observations favor better labels, broader independent evaluation and review of weak categories before a larger model or operational use.

Practical outcome. The project is suitable for teaching and supervised exploratory scrutiny. It does not yet justify automated public decisions. Explanations help a reviewer examine a suggestion; successful export checks establish that saved models reproduce predictions. Neither establishes correctness or fairness. A separate choropleth describes recorded project locations and programme themes, shared as italy_projects.html; geographic counts do not establish funding fairness or policy impact.

1. Original research proposal and hypotheses¶

The following proposal records the original motivation. The completed scope is exploratory title classification; funding and territorial analysis and independent human annotation were not completed.

1.1 The problem¶

I aim to make the distribution of Italy’s Piano Nazionale di Ripresa e Resilienza (PNRR) easier to understand: which activities receive funding, which organisations implement projects, and how resources are distributed across North, Centre, South, and Islands.

The opportunity for a neural network is to classify Italian project titles into meaningful purpose categories, such as digitalisation, infrastructure, education, and health. This could help when existing classifications are missing or too broad. Recorded categories will remain available alongside model predictions.

Funding totals and geographical comparisons will be calculated directly from the data. The network will predict a project category, not invent financial amounts or locations. The scope is the projects covered by the available data; complete coverage of all PNRR funds must be checked.

1.2. Why it matters¶

An understandable view of funding can support public transparency, help citizens explore investments in their area, and help researchers identify territorial and sectoral differences worth investigating. Keeping allocated funding separate from recorded payments also clarifies the difference between financing a project and spending money on it.

Differences in funding alone do not establish unfairness, misuse, or policy impact.

1.3. Appropriate data¶

The following files are used in this project

Local file Proposed use
data/progetti.csv Project titles, identifiers, PNRR financing, measure links, and implementing bodies
data/misure.csv and data/temi.csv Link measures to themes and define initial classification labels
data/progetti_territori.csv Locate projects and derive geographical groups
data/progetti_pagamenti.csv Analyse recorded PNRR payments and reporting dates separately from financing

OpenPNRR publishes these types of datasets and a field dictionary. Its documentation distinguishes finanziamento_pnrr from total project financing and pagamento_pnrr from total payments. It also defines the project field descrizione as the measure title, so this field should not be mistaken for an independent project description.

1.4. Proposed neural network¶

Start with a small multilayer perceptron (MLP): convert each Italian project title into TF–IDF numerical features, pass them through one or two hidden layers, and output probabilities for broad purpose categories.

Create initial labels by linking projects to measures and themes, then mapping themes to one broad category. These inherited labels are provisional: manually review a sample, resolve ambiguous mappings, and reserve an independently reviewed test sample. If reliable labels cannot be created, pause training and improve the annotation process.

Exclude measure names, measure codes, and identifiers from model inputs because they could reveal the target. Compare the network with a majority-class baseline and TF–IDF logistic regression. Neural networks are useful here only if they demonstrate value beyond these simpler approaches.

1.5. Research hypothesis and null hypothesis¶

Research question: Can a neural network classify the purpose of previously unseen PNRR projects from their titles more accurately than a simple text classifier?

H₁ — Alternative hypothesis: The MLP achieves higher expected macro-F1 than TF–IDF logistic regression on unseen, independently reviewed projects.

H₀ — Null hypothesis: The MLP achieves no higher expected macro-F1 than TF–IDF logistic regression on those projects.

Let $\Delta = F1_{\mathrm{macro,MLP}} - F1_{\mathrm{macro,logistic}}$.

$$H_0: \Delta \leq 0 \qquad H_1: \Delta > 0$$

Macro-F1 averages classification performance across categories so that large categories do not dominate the score. This hypothesis tests the model’s usefulness; it does not assume that North or South receives more funding.

1.6. What success would look like¶

  • Useful analysis: Reproducible tables and charts of PNRR financing and payments by purpose, implementing body, and geographical area, with unknown or unclassified amounts visible.
  • Useful model: A proposed target of test macro-F1 ≥ 0.80 and an improvement of at least 0.03 over logistic regression. These are project goals, not observed results.
  • Credible evaluation: Keep related measures, repeated projects, and duplicate titles together when splitting training, validation, and test data. Ensure each evaluated class has sufficient independent groups; use validation data for tuning and evaluate the frozen models once on the test set.
  • Hypothesis assessment: Estimate a paired bootstrap confidence interval for the macro-F1 difference, resampling independent groups. Reject H₀ at the 5% level only if the one-sided 95% lower confidence bound is above zero. Report uncertainty, class-level errors, and performance across territories.

If evidence is insufficient, fail to reject H₀; this does not prove that the models are equivalent. A reliable funding analysis remains valuable even if the neural network does not outperform the baseline.

1.7. Source references¶

  • OpenPNRR open-data catalogue — downloadable datasets; the publisher states that they use the ODbL 1.0 licence.
  • OpenPNRR metadata — field definitions and relationships.

Sources consulted on 25 September 2026. This consultation date does not establish the snapshot date of the local CSV files.

1.8 Completed research question and connected design rationale¶

The completed question is narrower than the original proposal: do nonlinear combinations of title terms (MLP), or learned local phrases (CNN), improve agreement with inherited programme themes over TF–IDF logistic regression on unseen connected programme groups? The input is a cleaned Italian title, the outcome is one retained ancestor theme, and the comparison is held-out macro-F1. The anticipated relationship is that local purpose terms may transfer across programmes, while programme templates and institution names may fail to transfer. This motivates training-only features, group isolation, a linear baseline and per-theme errors. The original human-reviewed-purpose hypothesis is retained as a future hypothesis; no independent annotation was completed in this notebook.

Three distinct sources contribute complementary concepts rather than added model complexity: OpenPNRR's metadata explains what the programme hierarchy and fields mean, constraining the target and excluding a measure description from independent text inputs; group-aware evaluation guidance explains why repeated programme examples must stay together; Kim's text-CNN research motivates a bounded test of local phrase order alongside the TF–IDF MLP. The SHAP framework adds a contestable word-level interpretation of the chosen MLP rather than a new performance objective.

Their contextual connection is the strategy: a simple title model under a harder programme-held-out test, with explicit weak-label uncertainty and human-review explanations. Novelty lies in fitting the evaluation and intended use to PNRR's administrative hierarchy; it is not a claim to invent a new architecture. These sources justify concepts and conventions, not the optimality of this notebook's hyperparameters or the truth of its inherited labels.

def seed_all(seed=SEED):
    random.seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    torch.set_num_threads(4)
    torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)

3. Load and preprocess the data¶

The three CSVs supply project titles and the measure/theme hierarchy needed for the completed classification task. Financial, payment and territorial fields are excluded because they do not answer the title classification question and would widen the experiment. Unicode normalization and retaining Italian accented letters reduce spelling variation without translating away the source language. Removing administrative codes, mixed letter/digit tokens and punctuation reduces identifier shortcuts; it also loses potentially meaningful numbers, so this is a documented trade-off rather than complete anonymization. Repeated spaces are collapsed to make duplicate detection consistent. The hierarchy cycle check stops invalid ancestry from silently producing incorrect labels.

In [4]:
def clean_title(value):
    text = unicodedata.normalize('NFKC', str(value)).lower()
    # Strip embedded mission/component/investment codes before punctuation removal.
    text = re.sub(r'\bm\s*\d+\s*c\s*\d+(?:\s*i\s*[\d.]+)?', ' ', text)
    # CUPs, local identifiers, dates, and numeric references are not language features.
    text = re.sub(r'\b\w*\d\w*\b', ' ', text)
    text = re.sub(r'[^a-zàèéìòóù\s]', ' ', text)
    return ' '.join(text.split())

def ancestor(key, parents):
    seen = set()
    while key in parents and pd.notna(parents[key]):
        if key in seen:
            raise ValueError('Cycle in source hierarchy')
        seen.add(key)
        key = int(parents[key])
    return int(key)

3.1 Validate joins and construct isolated groups¶

Why exclude, deduplicate and group? Many-to-one join validation prevents a hierarchy join from multiplying projects. Missing titles/measure matches and titles under three cleaned words cannot supply the intended inputs and targets. Identical cleaned titles with conflicting themes are removed because this title-only model cannot resolve their contradictory targets. Removing repeated titles limits the influence of administrative templates: the experiment estimates performance over unique titles, rather than weighting every repeated project equally.

The ancestor theme is a feasible weak label, not independently verified project purpose. A project can genuinely combine education, health or inclusion activities. At least 500 unique titles and six independent groups per retained theme are practical support rules, not statistically proven adequacy thresholds. Six groups allow at least two groups in each split; excluding smaller themes reduces coverage and requires an explicit unknown/review route.

Connected measure families, CUP identifiers and duplicate titles are kept together to prevent related examples from crossing split boundaries. This tests unfamiliar programme groups rather than memorization of a familiar template. The approximate 60/20/20 allocation balances training data with two held-out sets; uneven group sizes prevent exact proportions. Searching label/group-size balance, without model scores, avoids selecting a favorable test result. Group isolation takes priority over matching class proportions. The code stops on mixed-theme components rather than silently claiming a valid grouped split. This follows the rationale for group-aware cross-validation: dependent observations require dependent splits.

In [5]:
def prepare(data_dir, out, seed=42):
    out.mkdir(exist_ok=True, parents=True)
    audit = {'seed': seed, 'source_sha256': {},
             'minimum_class_titles': 500, 'minimum_class_groups': 6}
    for name in ['progetti', 'misure', 'temi']:
        path = data_dir / f'{name}.csv'
        audit['source_sha256'][path.name] = hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest()
    p = pd.read_csv(data_dir / 'progetti.csv', usecols=['progetto_id', 'titolo', 'cup', 'misura_id'])
    m = pd.read_csv(data_dir / 'misure.csv')
    t = pd.read_csv(data_dir / 'temi.csv')
    audit['raw_projects'] = len(p)
    audit['missing_titles'] = int(p.titolo.isna().sum())
    audit['duplicate_project_ids'] = int(p.progetto_id.duplicated().sum())
    if p.progetto_id.duplicated().any():
        raise ValueError('Resolve duplicate project IDs before proceeding')
    p = p.merge(m[['id', 'tema']], left_on='misura_id', right_on='id', how='left', validate='many_to_one')
    audit['unmatched_measure_ids'] = sorted(p.loc[p.tema.isna(), 'misura_id'].unique().tolist())
    audit['unmatched_measure_rows'] = int(p.tema.isna().sum())
    p = p.dropna(subset=['tema', 'titolo']).copy()
    theme_parents = t.set_index('id').parent_id.to_dict()
    measure_parents = m.set_index('id').madre_id.to_dict()
    names = t.set_index('id').descrizione.to_dict()
    p['label'] = p.tema.map(lambda x: names[ancestor(int(x), theme_parents)])
    p['family'] = p.misura_id.map(lambda x: ancestor(int(x), measure_parents))
    p['text'] = p.titolo.map(clean_title)
    short = p.text.str.split().str.len() < 3
    audit['titles_under_three_tokens'] = int(short.sum())
    p = p.loc[~short].copy()
    conflict = p.groupby('text').label.nunique()
    conflict = set(conflict[conflict > 1].index)
    audit['conflicting_title_strings'] = len(conflict)
    audit['conflicting_title_rows_removed'] = int(p.text.isin(conflict).sum())
    p = p.loc[~p.text.isin(conflict)].copy()
    # Union measure families when any remaining title or CUP links them.
    parents = {int(x): int(x) for x in p.family.unique()}

    def find(x):
        while parents[x] != x:
            parents[x] = parents[parents[x]]
            x = parents[x]
        return x

    def union(a, b):
        a, b = find(a), find(b)
        if a != b:
            parents[max(a, b)] = min(a, b)

    for col in ['text', 'cup']:
        first = {}
        for key, family in zip(p[col], p.family):
            if pd.isna(key) or not str(key).strip():
                continue
            if key in first:
                union(first[key], int(family))
            else:
                first[key] = int(family)
    p['group'] = p.family.map(find)
    audit['duplicate_clean_titles_removed'] = int(p.text.duplicated().sum())
    p = p.drop_duplicates('text').copy()
    support = p.groupby('label').agg(titles=('text', 'size'), independent_groups=('group', 'nunique'))
    audit['class_support_before_filter'] = support.reset_index().to_dict('records')
    eligible = support.index[(support.titles >= 500) & (support.independent_groups >= 6)]
    audit['excluded_classes'] = support.loc[~support.index.isin(eligible)].reset_index().to_dict('records')
    p = p[p.label.isin(eligible)].copy()
    if len(eligible) < 2:
        raise ValueError('Insufficient independent class groups for a defensible split')
    # Search labels/group sizes only, never model performance, for a feasible 60/20/20 split.
    labels = sorted(eligible)
    table = pd.crosstab(p.group, p.label).reindex(columns=labels, fill_value=0)
    counts = table.to_numpy()
    target = np.array([.6, .2, .2])
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    if np.any((counts > 0).sum(axis=1) != 1):
        raise ValueError('Mixed-label components require a joint group-split optimizer')
    assignment = np.zeros(len(table), dtype=int)
    class_errors = []
    for column in range(len(labels)):
        indices = np.flatnonzero(counts[:, column])
        n_holdout = max(2, round(len(indices) * .2))
        best = None
        for _ in range(5000):
            order = rng.permutation(indices)
            proposed = np.zeros(len(table), dtype=int)
            proposed[order[:n_holdout]] = 1
            proposed[order[n_holdout:2*n_holdout]] = 2
            parts = np.array([counts[indices[proposed[indices] == s], column].sum() for s in range(3)])
            if parts.min() < 20 or parts[0] < parts[1:].max():
                continue
            error = float(np.mean((parts / parts.sum() - target) ** 2))
            if best is None or error < best[0]:
                best = (error, proposed[indices].copy())
        if best is None:
            raise ValueError(f'No feasible split for {labels[column]}')
        assignment[indices] = best[1]
        class_errors.append(best[0])
    mapping = dict(zip(table.index, np.array(['train', 'validation', 'test'])[assignment]))
    p['split'] = p.group.map(mapping)
    audit['split_balance_error'] = float(np.mean(class_errors))
    audit['retained_unique_titles'] = len(p)
    audit['classes'] = labels
    audit['split_counts'] = pd.crosstab(p.label, p.split).to_dict()
    audit['split_group_counts'] = p.groupby(['split', 'label']).group.nunique().unstack().to_dict('index')
    for col in ['group', 'family', 'misura_id', 'cup', 'text']:
        if p.groupby(col).split.nunique().max() > 1:
            raise AssertionError(f'Split leakage: {col}')
    audit['leakage_assertions_passed'] = ['group', 'family', 'misura_id', 'cup', 'text']
    # Complete cleaned split manifest is preserved, even if training is subsampled later.
    cols = ['progetto_id', 'cup', 'misura_id', 'family', 'group', 'titolo', 'text', 'label', 'split']
    p[cols].to_csv(out / 'prepared_projects.csv.gz', index=False)
    (out / 'data_audit.json').write_text(json.dumps(audit, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False))
    print(f'Prepared {len(p):,} unique titles across {len(labels)} inherited themes.', flush=True)
    return p, audit

4. Training-only features and batched loading¶

Sample within the existing training and validation partitions, retaining every test title. Sparse TF–IDF becomes dense only for the current batch; the CNN uses padded/truncated token ID arrays.

Why a bounded experiment? The 24,000 training and 8,000 validation title limits make CPU execution feasible during the project. Class-stratified sampling preserves proportions within the already isolated partitions; it does not make all themes uniform or repair distribution shift. Retaining the complete test partition avoids a small convenience test sample. Sparse storage and converting only a current batch to dense TF–IDF reduce memory pressure; CNN token arrays have a fixed size. These are resource choices, not evidence that more training data would add no value.

In [7]:
def sample_partition(frame, limit):
    if limit is None or len(frame) <= limit:
        return frame.copy()
    chosen, _ = train_test_split(np.arange(len(frame)), train_size=limit, stratify=frame.label, random_state=SEED)
    return frame.iloc[chosen].copy()

def encode(texts, vocab, length=80):
    result = np.zeros((len(texts), length), dtype=np.int64)
    for i, text in enumerate(texts):
        ids = [vocab.get(w, 1) for w in text.split()[:length]]
        result[i, :len(ids)] = ids
    return result

def batch_tensor(x, idx):
    data = x[idx]
    if hasattr(data, 'toarray'):
        data = data.toarray()
    return torch.from_numpy(data)

def len_or_shape(x):
    return x.shape[0]

4.2 Fit TF–IDF and vocabulary on training titles¶

Validation and test titles are transformed without refitting. The saved vectorizer and vocabulary are outputs for later deployment; the notebook continues using the in-memory objects.

Why these representations? TF–IDF retains distinctive Italian purpose words; unigrams capture individual terms and bigrams capture short phrases. Sublinear term frequency limits repeated-word dominance, while min_df=2 removes one-off features. The 6,000-feature cap bounds MLP size. The CNN's at-most-12,000-token vocabulary and minimum frequency of two likewise bound its learned embedding matrix; a separate unknown token makes unseen language visible. Padding uses a separate zero ID, and the 80-word cutoff bounds computation. The diagnostics report actual truncation so this choice can be revisited if future titles are longer. These settings are practical starting choices, not tuned optima. Fitting both representations only on training titles prevents validation/test language from influencing the learned feature space. Saving fitted preprocessing preserves the same transformations at inference.

In [9]:
tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(max_features=6000, ngram_range=(1, 2), min_df=2, sublinear_tf=True, dtype=np.float32)
x_mlp = {'train': tfidf.fit_transform(texts['train'])}
x_mlp.update({s: tfidf.transform(texts[s]) for s in ['validation', 'test']})
word_counts = Counter(w for text in texts['train'] for w in text.split())
vocab = {'<PAD>': 0, '<UNK>': 1}
vocab.update({w: i + 2 for i, (w, count) in enumerate(word_counts.most_common(11998)) if count >= 2})
length = 80
x_cnn = {s: encode(texts[s], vocab, length) for s in texts}
with open(OUT / 'tfidf.pkl', 'wb') as f:
    pickle.dump(tfidf, f)
(OUT / 'vocabulary.json').write_text(json.dumps(vocab, ensure_ascii=False))

4.3 Record coverage and class weights¶

Unknown-token rates, class counts and independent-group counts expose distribution shift. Square-root inverse-frequency class weights reduce dominance by common categories.

Why weights and diagnostics? Square-root inverse-frequency weights reduce the training influence of common themes while tempering the stronger amplification of rare, potentially noisy labels under full inverse-frequency weighting. Normalizing weights to a mean of one keeps their scale readable. This does not guarantee equal errors across categories. Counts and independent groups describe different kinds of support; many similar titles cannot replace independent programmes. Unknown word rates expose vocabulary shift, and truncation rates expose lost tail text. A fixed, class-stratified 3,000-title training monitoring subset bounds repeated measurement cost; it estimates training behavior rather than reporting every training title each epoch. The full validation subset guides selection.

In [10]:

5. Explicit neural network architectures¶

B denotes batch size; F is the fitted TF–IDF feature count (at most 6,000), V the vocabulary (at most 12,000), and C the retained theme count (8 for these data).

MLP: float32 [B,F] → Linear(F,128) → ReLU → Dropout → Linear(128,64) → ReLU → Dropout → Linear(64,C) logits. The class below is the actual executable definition.

Why an MLP first? The inputs are short titles with sparse purpose terms, so a compact nonlinear network can test whether combinations of TF–IDF terms improve on a linear classifier. Two hidden layers of 128 and 64 units limit capacity and CPU cost; ReLU supplies the nonlinearity. These sizes are feasible design settings, not benchmark-proven best values for PNRR. Dropout is varied during the bounded comparison below. A simpler classifier remains an essential reference because a neural network is useful only if its quality or practical benefits justify it.

In [11]:
class TitleMLP(nn.Module):
    """Two hidden layers learn nonlinear combinations of TF-IDF features."""
    def __init__(self, n_features, n_classes, dropout=.4):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(n_features, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(dropout),
                                 nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(dropout),
                                 nn.Linear(64, n_classes))

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)

5.1 Text CNN¶

int64 [B,80] → Embedding(V,64) → parallel Conv1d(64,64,k=3/5) with same padding → ReLU → masked global max-pooling → concatenate [B,128] → Dropout → Linear(128,64) → ReLU → Dropout → Linear(64,C) logits. Masking prevents padded positions from winning the pool. Cross-entropy uses logits; softmax is applied during inference.

Why compare a CNN? Learned 64-dimensional word embeddings and three-/five-word convolution windows test whether local ordering and short phrases provide useful information beyond TF–IDF. Parallel windows handle more than one phrase length; max pooling detects a relevant phrase anywhere in a variable-length title. Padding masking prevents artificial padded positions from winning the pool. This is informed by Kim's text CNN, but these embeddings are learned from scratch and the paper's results do not validate this dataset. The chosen dimensions bound compute; they were not exhaustively tuned. Eight logits correspond to mutually exclusive retained programme themes. Cross-entropy consumes logits directly, and softmax is reserved for scores at evaluation/inference.

Alternative Decision and reason
Majority prediction Retained as a minimal no-language reference, fixed from training counts.
TF–IDF logistic regression Retained as a cheap, interpretable linear text benchmark using the same titles/splits.
RNN/LSTM Not implemented: sequential processing adds cost, while short titles make local phrases a reasonable first ordering test. Its quality is unknown here.
Pretrained Italian/multilingual transformer Deferred: potentially useful semantic transfer, especially under vocabulary shift, but additional weights, dependencies and compute widen the CPU experiment. No inferiority claim is made.
Larger MLP/CNN or long-document architecture Deferred until reliable labels and current errors justify more capacity; extra complexity cannot resolve an ambiguous target by itself.

The MLP/CNN comparison balances conventional text modeling with feasibility; it is not a claim to state-of-the-art predictive performance.

In [12]:
class TitleCNN(nn.Module):
    """Learn embeddings and local 3/5-token patterns; masked global max pooling."""
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, n_classes, dropout=.4):
        super().__init__()
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, 64, padding_idx=0)
        self.convs = nn.ModuleList([nn.Conv1d(64, 64, k, padding=k // 2) for k in (3, 5)])
        self.head = nn.Sequential(nn.Dropout(dropout), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(),
                                  nn.Dropout(dropout), nn.Linear(64, n_classes))

    def forward(self, x):
        valid = (x != 0).unsqueeze(1)
        emb = self.embedding(x).transpose(1, 2)
        pooled = [torch.relu(conv(emb)).masked_fill(~valid, -1e4).amax(dim=2) for conv in self.convs]
        return self.head(torch.cat(pooled, dim=1))

5.2 Verify layer shapes and padding behaviour¶

Instantiate both models, display their real structures, and check forward-pass dimensions before training.

What these checks establish. Shape checks catch wiring errors before training; adding only right-padding must not alter a CNN prediction. The cleaning assertion confirms one intended identifier-removal example. These are implementation checks, not evidence of semantic accuracy, privacy protection or robustness to every title.

6. Training, validation and model selection¶

Batched inference and metrics are defined below. Macro-F1 gives every retained class equal weight; accuracy weights titles.

Why these measures? Macro-F1 averages the precision/recall balance of each retained theme equally, making weak small-theme performance harder to hide. Accuracy answers how often a title receives its inherited label and can be dominated by prevalent themes. Unweighted log-loss assesses the whole score distribution and penalizes confident mistakes, so a model can improve class predictions while worsening probability performance. None measures verified project purpose without independent annotation. The validation set guides configuration/checkpoint selection; the test set assesses frozen choices.

In [14]:
@torch.inference_mode()
def predict(model, x, batch_size=512):
    model.eval()
    return np.concatenate([model(batch_tensor(x, np.arange(i, min(i + batch_size, len_or_shape(x)))))
                           .softmax(dim=1).numpy() for i in range(0, len_or_shape(x), batch_size)])

def scores(y, probs):
    pred = probs.argmax(axis=1)
    return {'accuracy': float(accuracy_score(y, pred)),
            'macro_f1': float(f1_score(y, pred, average='macro', labels=np.arange(probs.shape[1]), zero_division=0)),
            'loss': float(log_loss(y, probs, labels=np.arange(probs.shape[1])))}

6.1 Define the training loop¶

AdamW, weighted cross-entropy, gradient clipping, learning-rate scheduling and early stopping use validation macro-F1. The best checkpoint is restored. Histories stay in memory and are also written as output CSVs.

Why this optimization policy? Weighted cross-entropy fits one inherited theme per title. AdamW uses adaptive updates with separate weight decay, while clipping gradient norm at one bounds occasional large updates. An initial learning rate of 0.001 and batch size of 256 are feasible starting settings, not demonstrated optima. ReduceLROnPlateau halves the rate after validation macro-F1 stagnation (patience one), permitting smaller updates without spending a broad learning-rate search. The 14-epoch ceiling bounds compute; stopping after three unimproved epochs and restoring the best validation checkpoint limit degradation from continued fitting. The 0.0001 improvement tolerance avoids treating negligible score movement as a fresh improvement. Seeded shuffling makes the order reproducible within the recorded environment. Weighted optimization loss and unweighted evaluation loss answer different questions and should not be treated as directly comparable values.

In [15]:
def fit_neural(name, model, xtrain, ytrain, xval, yval, weights, cfg, monitor_idx):
    seed_all()
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=cfg['lr'], weight_decay=cfg['weight_decay'])
    scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.ReduceLROnPlateau(optimizer, mode='max', factor=.5, patience=1)
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(weight=torch.tensor(weights, dtype=torch.float32))
    ytensor = torch.tensor(ytrain, dtype=torch.long)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    history, best, best_epoch, stale = [], -1., 0, 0
    start = time.perf_counter()
    for epoch in range(1, cfg['max_epochs'] + 1):
        epoch_start = time.perf_counter()
        model.train()
        order = rng.permutation(len(ytrain))
        optimization_loss = 0.
        lr = optimizer.param_groups[0]['lr']
        for offset in range(0, len(order), cfg['batch_size']):
            idx = order[offset:offset + cfg['batch_size']]
            optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
            logits = model(batch_tensor(xtrain, idx))
            loss = criterion(logits, ytensor[idx])
            loss.backward()
            nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.)
            optimizer.step()
            optimization_loss += loss.item() * len(idx)
        train_metrics = scores(ytrain[monitor_idx], predict(model, xtrain[monitor_idx]))
        val_metrics = scores(yval, predict(model, xval))
        row = {'epoch': epoch, 'lr': lr, 'optimization_loss': optimization_loss / len(ytrain),
               **{'train_' + k: v for k, v in train_metrics.items()},
               **{'val_' + k: v for k, v in val_metrics.items()},
               'seconds': time.perf_counter() - epoch_start}
        history.append(row)
        pd.DataFrame(history).to_csv(OUT / f'{name}_history.csv', index=False)
        print(f"{name:18} epoch={epoch:02} train_loss={row['train_loss']:.4f} "
              f"val_loss={row['val_loss']:.4f} val_acc={row['val_accuracy']:.4f} "
              f"val_F1={row['val_macro_f1']:.4f} lr={lr:.5f} seconds={row['seconds']:.1f}", flush=True)
        if val_metrics['macro_f1'] > best + 1e-4:
            best, best_epoch, stale = val_metrics['macro_f1'], epoch, 0
            best_state = copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())
        else:
            stale += 1
        scheduler.step(val_metrics['macro_f1'])
        if stale >= cfg['patience']:
            break
    model.load_state_dict(best_state)
    torch.save({'state_dict': best_state, 'config': cfg, 'best_epoch': best_epoch}, OUT / f'{name}.pt')
    result = {'name': name, **cfg, 'best_epoch': best_epoch, 'epochs_run': len(history),
              'seconds': time.perf_counter() - start,
              'parameters': sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()),
              'validation': scores(yval, predict(model, xval)),
              'last_epoch_validation_f1': history[-1]['val_macro_f1'],
              'lr_reductions': sum(history[i]['lr'] < history[i - 1]['lr'] for i in range(1, len(history)))}
    return model, result, pd.DataFrame(history)

6.2 Tune the logistic regression baseline¶

Choose C using validation data only. The majority baseline is defined from training class counts.

Why a fair simple reference? Logistic regression uses the same fitted TF–IDF features and partitions, so the comparison tests the value of nonlinear modeling without adding different input information. Validation selects between C=0.5 and C=2.0 (different regularization strengths). These two settings are a bounded search, not full optimization. Balanced class weights support the minority-theme objective, but use full inverse-frequency weighting rather than the neural models' square-root weighting; therefore the losses are not identical. The iteration cap bounds fitting effort. The majority category is fixed from training data, since choosing the test-majority category would use held-out labels improperly.

In [16]:
# Baseline tuning uses validation only.
start = time.perf_counter()
baselines = []
for c in [0.5, 2.0]:
    clf = LogisticRegression(C=c, class_weight='balanced', max_iter=400, solver='lbfgs', random_state=SEED)
    clf.fit(x_mlp['train'], y['train'])
    result = {'C': c, 'validation': scores(y['validation'], clf.predict_proba(x_mlp['validation']))}
    results['baseline_tuning'].append(result)
    baselines.append(clf)
best_i = max(range(len(baselines)), key=lambda i: results['baseline_tuning'][i]['validation']['macro_f1'])
logistic = baselines[best_i]
results['logistic_seconds_including_tuning'] = time.perf_counter() - start
results['logistic_selected_C'] = results['baseline_tuning'][best_i]['C']
with open(OUT / 'logistic.pkl', 'wb') as f:
    pickle.dump(logistic, f)

6.3 Train the four neural configurations¶

Compare plain models (dropout 0, weight decay 0) with regularized models (dropout 0.4, weight decay 0.0001). This tests their combined effect. Training progress is printed each epoch; all histories remain available in memory. Model choices are made before viewing test predictions.

Why only four runs? For each architecture, the plain and regularized variants compare no dropout/decay with dropout 0.4 plus weight decay 0.0001 under the same seed and budget. This examines their combined effect and cannot isolate which component caused a difference. Validation macro-F1 selects each architecture's variant and then the leading neural architecture. A single seed and two variants are a systematic but narrow comparison: observed gains are not proof of a global optimum or stable superiority. The learning curves and final briefing explain whether continued training brought diminishing returns or overfitting.

In [17]:
chosen_models, histories = {}, {}
for kind, features in [('mlp', x_mlp), ('cnn', x_cnn)]:
    candidates = {}
    for variant, dropout, decay in [('plain', 0., 0.), ('regularized', .4, 1e-4)]:
        seed_all()
        model = (TitleMLP(features['train'].shape[1], len(classes), dropout) if kind == 'mlp'
                 else TitleCNN(len(vocab), len(classes), dropout))
        name = f'{kind}_{variant}'
        cfg = {'kind': kind, 'dropout': dropout, 'weight_decay': decay, 'lr': .001,
               'batch_size': 256, 'max_epochs': EPOCHS, 'patience': 3}
        model, result, history = fit_neural(name, model, features['train'], y['train'], features['validation'],
                                   y['validation'], weights, cfg, monitor_idx)
        results['runs'][name] = result
        histories[name] = history
        candidates[name] = model
        (OUT / 'results_in_progress.json').write_text(json.dumps(results, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False))
    selected = max(candidates, key=lambda n: results['runs'][n]['validation']['macro_f1'])
    results['selected'][kind.upper()] = selected
    chosen_models[kind.upper()] = candidates[selected]

6.4 Paired group bootstrap¶

Resample whole test groups jointly for both classifiers. The few independent groups make these intervals exploratory; an absent class receives F1=0 in a replicate.

Why resample groups together? Related titles share programme wording, so a row-level bootstrap would overstate independent information. Jointly resampling whole groups preserves the pairing between classifiers on the same observations. The 1,000 seeded resamples bound computation and provide an exploratory uncertainty summary; more titles do not remove the limitation of few groups. Keeping all eight categories in every replicate, with absent-category F1 set to zero, avoids quietly changing the definition of macro-F1, but makes the interval sensitive to scarce classes. An interval containing zero does not support a positive difference; it also does not prove equivalence. These weak-label intervals cannot test the proposal's hypothesis about independently reviewed purposes.

In [18]:
def group_bootstrap(y, pred_a, pred_b, groups, classes, n_boot=1000):
    """Paired cluster bootstrap: cache per-group confusion matrices for efficiency."""
    matrices = []
    for group in np.unique(groups):
        idx = groups == group
        matrices.append([confusion_matrix(y[idx], pred[idx], labels=np.arange(classes)) for pred in (pred_a, pred_b)])
    matrices = np.array(matrices)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    deltas = []
    for _ in range(n_boot):
        cm = matrices[rng.integers(len(matrices), size=len(matrices))].sum(axis=0)
        f1 = 2 * np.diagonal(cm, axis1=1, axis2=2) / np.maximum(cm.sum(axis=1) + cm.sum(axis=2), 1)
        deltas.append(float(f1[0].mean() - f1[1].mean()))
    return {'point_difference': float(f1_score(y, pred_a, average='macro') - f1_score(y, pred_b, average='macro')),
            'ci95': np.quantile(deltas, [.025, .975]).tolist(),
            'one_sided_95_lower': float(np.quantile(deltas, .05)),
            'replicates': n_boot, 'independent_test_groups': len(matrices),
            'caveat': 'Few groups per class; absent classes get F1=0 in a replicate. Interval is exploratory.'}

7. Held-out evaluation and verification¶

Freeze selected checkpoints first. Evaluate the complete test partition once, retaining per-title predictions and per-class metrics as output files. All objects used below were created in this kernel.

Why freeze and retain outputs? Writing selected configurations before test prediction makes the selection sequence inspectable. Complete test predictions, per-class reports and group-paired intervals reveal failures concealed by one average. A hard majority prediction is not a useful probability model, so its log-loss is omitted rather than compared with softmax distributions. The result briefing is calculated from current-run objects so numerical conclusions follow any rerun rather than remaining fixed in prose.

7.1 Check split boundaries and recompute reported metrics¶

These executable assertions check the current data, not a saved claim that checks passed.

What passing means. The assertions verify observed identity/group isolation, complete held-out membership and arithmetic agreement with saved prediction rows. They reduce implementation-error risk; they do not establish representative source coverage, independent label validity or deployment fairness.

7.2 Plot the current run¶

Editable plotting code uses the in-memory histories and predictions. Train metrics use the fixed monitoring subset with dropout off; plotted losses are unweighted evaluation losses. Optimization loss in the histories is weighted training loss.

Why these three visual views? Learning curves show the cost and benefit of additional epochs; falling training loss with rising validation loss warns of fitting patterns that do not transfer. The model bars compare a title-weighted measure with an equal-category measure. Row-normalized confusion matrices display where each source theme is routed, even if it has few test titles; a large diagonal entry is recall, not proof of precision. Fixed 0–1 performance scales, numerical annotations and separate training/validation lines support comparison. Curves motivate early stopping/restoration; class errors motivate label review and a supervised use boundary. Numerical interpretation is provided in the final briefing.

In [21]:
def plots(results, classes, ytest, probabilities, histories):
    plt.rcParams.update({'figure.dpi': 140, 'font.size': 10, 'axes.spines.top': False, 'axes.spines.right': False})
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(16, 8), constrained_layout=True)
    for row, kind in enumerate(['mlp', 'cnn']):
        for variant, style in [('plain', '--'), ('regularized', '-')]:
            h = histories[f'{kind}_{variant}']
            for split, color in [('train', '#26749c'), ('val', '#d47732')]:
                axes[row, 0].plot(h.epoch, h[f'{split}_loss'], style, color=color, label=f'{variant}: {split}')
                axes[row, 1].plot(h.epoch, h[f'{split}_macro_f1'], style, color=color, label=f'{variant}: {split}')
                axes[row, 2].plot(h.epoch, h[f'{split}_accuracy'], style, color=color, label=f'{variant}: {split}')
        axes[row, 0].set(title=f'{kind.upper()} — cross-entropy', xlabel='Epoch', ylabel='Unweighted loss')
        axes[row, 1].set(title=f'{kind.upper()} — macro-F1', xlabel='Epoch', ylabel='Macro-F1', ylim=(0, 1))
        axes[row, 2].set(title=f'{kind.upper()} — accuracy', xlabel='Epoch', ylabel='Accuracy', ylim=(0, 1))
        for ax in axes[row]:
            ax.legend(fontsize=8)
            ax.grid(alpha=.2)
    fig.savefig(OUT / 'training_curves.png')

7.3 Inspect class-level performance and confident errors¶

Aggregate accuracy conceals large category differences. These are errors against inherited labels, not verified human annotations.

Why inspect confident disagreements? Class-level precision, recall and F1 identify themes where a good overall average could still mislead stakeholders. Sorting disagreements by score deliberately finds warning examples, not a representative error sample. A university-named health project can activate education language, and an inclusion project can describe a school activity. These cases can reflect a shortcut, ambiguous wording or disagreement between programme and activity labels; human review is needed to distinguish them. Near-one scores on disagreements show why softmax must not be interpreted as a verified probability of being correct. The bootstrap interpretation and current class disparities are stated in the final briefing.

7.4 Explain individual MLP predictions with SHAP¶

Question: which words contribute to the MLP's score for a particular theme? We explain the MLP checkpoint selected by validation macro-F1 in section 6; this does not explain the CNN or change either model. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) allocates a prediction's difference from a reference among input features, averaging their marginal contributions across feature coalitions.

Here a feature is a word occurrence in the cleaned title, identified by its position. A binary mask includes or deletes each occurrence; retained words keep their order. Each masked title passes through the already fitted TF–IDF vectorizer and MLP, so explanations include preprocessing effects, including changed bigrams and TF–IDF normalization. We use the model-agnostic PermutationExplainer with an Independent masker whose single background row is all zeros. This defines a word-deletion game with an empty-title reference, not an average training title or a population prior.

For theme $c$ and cleaned title $x$, the identity link gives

$$p_c(x) = p_c(\text{empty title}) + \sum_{j=1}^{m}\phi_{j,c}.$$

Positive contributions increase that theme's softmax score relative to the empty title; negative contributions decrease it. Values multiplied by 100 are percentage points, not relative percent changes, causal effects, or calibrated probabilities of correctness. The code checks this reconstruction for all eight outputs. It uses 20 forward/reverse permutation cycles per example and repeats with another seed to assess approximation sensitivity. Additivity alone does not establish that the individual estimates have converged.

For a bounded, reproducible demonstration, take the lowest project ID among test titles of 3–30 cleaned words in each of two strata: agreement and disagreement with the inherited theme. This deliberately selected pair is a local diagnostic, not a representative sample or a global feature-importance estimate. Labels are used only to select the diagnostic cases after training and model selection; no parameters are changed.

Why this method rather than another explanation? A model-agnostic word-deletion SHAP game explains the whole fitted TF–IDF/MLP pipeline in words a reviewer can inspect, including changes in bigrams and normalization. The SHAP framework supplies the additive contribution logic, not evidence that these weak labels or masking choices are correct.

Explanation option Use and trade-off in this task
Logistic coefficients Cheap, readable global associations, but explain the linear baseline rather than the nonlinear MLP or an individual full-pipeline prediction.
Permutation SHAP (chosen) Readable local word contributions with an explicit reference/reconstruction; repeated model calls cost more and deletion can create unnatural titles.
Integrated gradients Appropriate for differentiable neural representations and potentially cheaper repeated explanation; discrete cleaning/TF–IDF complicates end-to-end word attribution, and a reference/path still needs justification.
LIME A local surrogate can be readable, but its sampling/neighborhood and surrogate fidelity add choices; it does not implement this same additive allocation game.

For reviewers, readable evidence for challenging a suggestion is more useful than an unexplained hidden-unit signal. For affected communities, a contestable source category and correction route matter more than a persuasive plot. Only two purposefully selected MLP examples are explained: this cannot establish global importance, population fairness or CNN interpretability.

In [23]:
SHAP_CYCLES, SHAP_MAX_WORDS = 20, 30
shap_model_kind = 'MLP'
shap_selected_run = r['selected'][shap_model_kind]

def shap_text_scores(texts):
    # Empty/short strings are permitted only for the explanatory deletion game.
    # The deployment function still rejects invalid user inputs.
    cleaned = [clean_title(str(text)) for text in texts]
    features = tfidf.transform(cleaned)
    return predict(chosen_models[shap_model_kind], features, batch_size=128)

                                    on='progetto_id', validate='one_to_one')
shap_candidates = shap_candidates[shap_candidates.text.str.split().str.len().between(3, SHAP_MAX_WORDS)]
shap_candidates = shap_candidates.sort_values('progetto_id', kind='stable')
shap_agreement = shap_candidates[shap_model_kind + '_prediction'] == shap_candidates.label
shap_cases = pd.concat([
    shap_candidates.loc[shap_agreement].head(1).assign(case='Label agreement'),
    shap_candidates.loc[~shap_agreement].head(1).assign(case='Label disagreement')
]).reset_index(drop=True)
assert len(shap_cases), 'No eligible held-out title for the SHAP demonstration'

    print('Only one diagnostic stratum is available in this run.')

7.4.1 Compute contributions and verify the explanation¶

The first seed supplies the displayed contributions. A second seed provides a sensitivity check, not a confidence interval. Prediction scores must agree with the held-out evaluation before interpreting either explanation. All per-word/per-class values, case IDs, settings, and diagnostics are saved in this run's output folder.

Why bound and repeat the calculation? Three to 30 words and 20 permutation cycles limit explanation cost. Selecting the lowest ID in agreement/disagreement strata makes case selection reproducible without optimizing the model. Repeating with a second seed checks finite-sampling sensitivity; arithmetic reconstruction and prediction parity check that the explanation matches the evaluated model. None validates the empty-title reference, estimates causal effects or certifies convergence. Saved case IDs/settings/contributions make a reviewer able to inspect the explanation choices rather than only the rendered bars.

In [24]:
def explain_word_deletions(text, seed):
    words = text.split()
    feature_names = [f'{position + 1}: {word}' for position, word in enumerate(words)]
    def score_masks(masks):
        masked_texts = [' '.join(word for word, present in zip(words, mask) if present)
                        for mask in masks]
        return shap_text_scores(masked_texts)
    masker = shap.maskers.Independent(np.zeros((1, len(words)), dtype=np.float32))
    explainer = shap.PermutationExplainer(score_masks, masker, feature_names=feature_names,
                                        seed=seed, output_names=classes)
    return explainer(np.ones((1, len(words)), dtype=np.float32),
                     max_evals=SHAP_CYCLES * (2 * len(words) + 1),
                     batch_size=128, silent=True)[0]

shap_started = time.perf_counter()
shap_explanations, shap_diagnostics, shap_rows = [], [], []
for case in shap_cases.itertuples(index=False):
    explanation = explain_word_deletions(case.text, SEED)
    repeated = explain_word_deletions(case.text, SEED + 1)
    full_scores = shap_text_scores([case.text])[0]
    empty_scores = shap_text_scores([''])[0]
    assert explanation.values.shape == (len(case.text.split()), len(classes))
    assert np.isfinite(explanation.values).all()
    for estimate in [explanation, repeated]:
        np.testing.assert_allclose(estimate.base_values, empty_scores, atol=1e-6, rtol=1e-5)
        np.testing.assert_allclose(estimate.base_values + estimate.values.sum(axis=0),
                                   full_scores, atol=1e-6, rtol=1e-5)
    predicted_class = int(full_scores.argmax())
    assert classes[predicted_class] == case.MLP_prediction
    np.testing.assert_allclose(full_scores[predicted_class], case.MLP_confidence,
                               atol=1e-6, rtol=1e-5)
    values = explanation.values[:, predicted_class]
    repeat_values = repeated.values[:, predicted_class]
    top_k = min(3, len(values))
    top = set(np.argsort(np.abs(values))[-top_k:])
    repeat_top = set(np.argsort(np.abs(repeat_values))[-top_k:])
    shap_diagnostics.append({
        'case': case.case, 'progetto_id': int(case.progetto_id),
        'predicted_theme': classes[predicted_class], 'inherited_theme': case.label,
        'base_score': float(explanation.base_values[predicted_class]),
        'sum_contributions': float(values.sum()),
        'predicted_score': float(full_scores[predicted_class]),
        'max_reconstruction_error_all_classes': float(np.max(np.abs(
            explanation.base_values + explanation.values.sum(axis=0) - full_scores))),
        'max_seed_change_pp_predicted_class': float(100 * np.max(np.abs(values - repeat_values))),
        'top_3_word_positions_shared_across_seeds': len(top & repeat_top)})
    shap_explanations.append(explanation)
    for position, word in enumerate(case.text.split()):
        for class_index, theme in enumerate(classes):
            shap_rows.append({'progetto_id': int(case.progetto_id), 'case': case.case,
                              'word_position': position + 1, 'word': word, 'theme': theme,
                              'shap_value': float(explanation.values[position, class_index]),
                              'repeat_seed_value': float(repeated.values[position, class_index]),
                              'base_score': float(explanation.base_values[class_index]),
                              'predicted_score': float(full_scores[class_index])})
shap_diagnostics = pd.DataFrame(shap_diagnostics)
shap_metadata = {'shap_version': shap.__version__, 'model': shap_model_kind,
                 'selected_run': shap_selected_run, 'seeds': [SEED, SEED + 1],

7.4.2 Read the local explanations¶

Each chart explains the predicted theme, including for the disagreement case. Blue positive bars raise its score; orange negative bars lower it. Word positions distinguish repeated words. The 12 largest absolute contributions are shown individually; any remaining contributions are summed into one labelled bar so nothing is silently discarded. Both charts use a common horizontal scale. The full title and all contributions remain available above and in the exported CSVs.

7.5 Real-world implication: transparency without false reassurance¶

Imagine this classifier helping an analyst route PNRR projects to thematic reviewers or build a public dashboard. SHAP can make a suggested category contestable: the analyst can inspect which title words support it, compare the recorded programme theme, and flag reliance on an institution name or administrative phrase. The disagreement example above shows why explanations should accompany difficult cases as well as successful ones. A disagreement is not automatically a model error: the inherited label may describe the programme while the title describes a different activity.

The central risk is false reassurance. A fluent-looking explanation can make an uncertain classification seem justified. This model learns agreement with weak programme labels; SHAP explains that learned scoring behaviour, not a project's actual purpose, eligibility, public value, or entitlement to funding. A large positive word contribution therefore cannot justify overwriting the source category. Conversely, a small attribution does not prove a word is irrelevant in every context, or that geographic and organizational proxies are absent. Two examples cannot establish population-wide transparency or fairness.

The explanation itself embeds choices. Deleting words can create unnatural titles and new adjacent bigrams, and TF–IDF normalization changes when the text changes. The empty title is outside the training population. These attributions answer a specific word-deletion question; a different reference, token grouping, output class, or score scale can allocate importance differently. The seed check measures only finite-permutation variation, while the reconstruction check establishes arithmetic consistency. Neither validates the masking assumption or turns the contributions into causal effects. Softmax also couples the classes, so a contribution to one class's score can reflect changes in competing class scores. This section explains the MLP only.

Practical consequence. A review interface should show the original and cleaned title, inherited theme, suggested theme, uncalibrated score, model version, and explanation settings together, and allow the reviewer to retain or challenge the suggestion. Before operational use, test whether explanations help reviewers detect mistakes across themes, title styles and organizations, using independently reviewed labels; record corrections and check whether confident-looking plots instead increase acceptance of errors. Use wider stratified explanation audits and alternative masking choices to investigate shortcuts. The defensible role of SHAP here is to support scrutiny and correction, with a human retaining responsibility for decisions—not to certify correctness or fairness.

7.6 Current-run results and decision interpretation¶

The following interpretation is computed from the same histories, held-out predictions and explanation diagnostics as the figures. It connects each outcome to the model-selection and intended-use decisions; no extra training is performed.

def technical_result_brief(r, audit, report, histories, shap_diagnostics):
    """Explain current-run results using only already computed notebook objects."""
    selected = max(r['selected'], key=lambda k: r['runs'][r['selected'][k]]['validation']['macro_f1'])
    scores_now = r['test'][selected]
    logistic_now = r['test']['Logistic']
    mlp_delta = r['bootstrap_mlp_minus_logistic']
    cnn_delta = r['bootstrap_cnn_minus_mlp']
    class_rows = report[(report.model == selected) & report.category.isin(r['classes'])].copy()
    strongest = class_rows.loc[class_rows['f1-score'].idxmax()]
    weakest = class_rows.loc[class_rows['f1-score'].idxmin()]
    train_counts = r['diagnostics']['train']['class_counts']
    test_counts = r['diagnostics']['test']['class_counts']
    majority_theme = max(train_counts, key=train_counts.get)
    majority_share = test_counts.get(majority_theme, 0) / r['diagnostics']['test']['rows']
    interval = mlp_delta['ci95']
    gain = mlp_delta['point_difference']
    selected_gain = scores_now['macro_f1'] - logistic_now['macro_f1']
    target_status = 'met' if scores_now['macro_f1'] >= .80 else 'not met'
    gain_status = 'met' if selected_gain >= .03 else 'not met'
    interval_reading = ('does not support a reliable positive difference' if interval[0] <= 0 <= interval[1]
                        else 'suggests a positive difference under these resampling assumptions' if interval[0] > 0
                        else 'suggests a negative difference under these resampling assumptions')
    lower_reading = ('above zero' if mlp_delta['one_sided_95_lower'] > 0 else 'not above zero')
    excluded = ', '.join(item['label'] for item in audit['excluded_classes']) or 'none in this run'
    optimization_rows, curve_readings = [], []
    for name, run in r['runs'].items():
        h = histories[name]
        optimization_rows.append(
            f"| {name.replace('_', ' ')} | {run['validation']['macro_f1']:.3f} | "
            f"{run['best_epoch']} / {run['epochs_run']} | {run['lr_reductions']} | {run['seconds']:.2f} |")
        if h.iloc[-1]['train_loss'] < h.iloc[0]['train_loss'] and h.iloc[-1]['val_loss'] > h.iloc[0]['val_loss']:
            curve_readings.append(name.replace('_', ' '))
    neural_seconds = sum(run['seconds'] for run in r['runs'].values())
    mlp_seconds = sum(run['seconds'] for name, run in r['runs'].items() if name.startswith('mlp_'))
    cnn_seconds = sum(run['seconds'] for name, run in r['runs'].items() if name.startswith('cnn_'))
    cost_ratio = cnn_seconds / mlp_seconds if mlp_seconds > 0 else float('nan')
    mlp_plain = r['runs']['mlp_plain']['validation']['macro_f1']
    mlp_reg = r['runs']['mlp_regularized']['validation']['macro_f1']
    cnn_plain = r['runs']['cnn_plain']['validation']['macro_f1']
    cnn_reg = r['runs']['cnn_regularized']['validation']['macro_f1']
    logloss_gap = r['test']['MLP']['loss'] - logistic_now['loss']
    loss_reading = ('worse' if logloss_gap > 0 else 'better' if logloss_gap < 0 else 'equal')
    shap_seed = float(shap_diagnostics.max_seed_change_pp_predicted_class.max())
    shap_shared = int(shap_diagnostics.top_3_word_positions_shared_across_seeds.min())
    shap_error = float(shap_diagnostics.max_reconstruction_error_all_classes.max())
    curve_text = (', '.join(curve_readings) +
                  ' fit their training titles better while their validation loss rose. This warns that continued fitting can strengthen patterns that fail on unfamiliar programmes.'
                  if curve_readings else
                  'The curves should be read together: improvements on training titles alone do not establish transfer to unfamiliar programmes.')
    text = [
        f"**What was completed.** From {audit['raw_projects']:,} source project rows, cleaning retained "
        f"{audit['retained_unique_titles']:,} unique titles across {len(r['classes'])} themes. "
        f"The experiment used {r['diagnostics']['train']['rows']:,} training titles, "
        f"{r['diagnostics']['validation']['rows']:,} validation titles and "
        f"{r['diagnostics']['test']['rows']:,} test titles. Related programme groups stayed together. "
        "Training/validation were sampled to keep CPU work feasible; the full held-out title set was evaluated. "
        f"Excluded themes: **{excluded}**. Exclusion reflects insufficient independent support, not lesser public importance. "
        "Removing duplicates reduces template memorization but changes the population to unique titles. "
        "Financial allocation, recorded payments, territorial fairness and independently reviewed purposes were not evaluated by this model.",
        f"**How well it worked.** Validation selected **{selected}**; its held-out accuracy was "
        f"**{scores_now['accuracy']:.1%}** and its equal-theme score was **{scores_now['macro_f1']:.3f}**. "
        f"Logistic regression achieved {logistic_now['accuracy']:.1%} accuracy and {logistic_now['macro_f1']:.3f} macro-F1. "
        f"The proposed 0.80 equal-theme target was **{target_status}**, and the selected neural model's "

        "These goals were chosen for the project, not independently established deployment thresholds.",
        f"**What uncertainty allows us to say.** MLP minus logistic regression was {gain:+.4f} macro-F1. "
        f"Its exploratory 95% interval was [{interval[0]:+.4f}, {interval[1]:+.4f}], which {interval_reading}. "

        f"CNN minus MLP was {cnn_delta['point_difference']:+.4f}, with interval "

        f"**Where it struggles.** {selected}'s strongest theme was **{strongest['category']}** "
        f"(F1 {strongest['f1-score']:.3f}, {int(strongest['support']):,} test titles) and weakest was "

        "A successful large theme cannot justify automatic treatment of every theme. "
        "The confusion matrices show where recorded themes are redirected; confident disagreement examples "
        "suggest possible reliance on institutional wording or ambiguity between overlapping activities. "
        "Those cases need targeted explanation and domain review. "
        "Some disagreements may expose ambiguous programme labels rather than an incorrect description of actual activity.",
        f"**Why the simplest reference can look unusually poor.** The training-majority theme was "
        f"**{majority_theme}**, but it represented only {majority_share:.1%} of held-out titles. "
        f"Always choosing it therefore gave {r['test']['Majority']['accuracy']:.1%} test accuracy. "
        "This reflects the changed mix of programmes under group isolation; it is not evidence that every "

        f"Unknown CNN words rose from {r['diagnostics']['train']['oov_token_rate']:.1%} in training to "

        f"versus {logistic_now['loss']:.3f} for logistic regression (lower is better), so MLP was {loss_reading} "
        "on this measure. Better theme assignments can coexist with poorer scores on confident errors. "
        "A displayed 90% model score is not evidence that 90 of 100 similar suggestions will be correct. "
        "Calibration and an independently validated review/abstention policy are needed before operational use.",
        "**What training choices achieved.** The table shows the selected checkpoint rather than assuming the last "
        "epoch was best. Both the rate reductions and early stopping followed validation behavior.\n\n"
        "| Configuration | Validation equal-theme score | Best epoch / epochs run | Rate reductions | Timed seconds |\n"
        "|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n" + '\n'.join(optimization_rows) + '\n\n' +
        f"Combined dropout/weight decay changed MLP validation macro-F1 from {mlp_plain:.3f} to {mlp_reg:.3f}, "
        f"and CNN from {cnn_plain:.3f} to {cnn_reg:.3f}; the selected variants were "
        f"{r['selected']['MLP'].replace('_', ' ')} and {r['selected']['CNN'].replace('_', ' ')}. "
        "This does not isolate dropout from weight decay or establish an optimal setting. " + curve_text +
        f" CNN's two fits took {cnn_seconds/60:.2f} minutes versus {mlp_seconds:.2f} seconds for the two MLP fits "
        f"(about {cost_ratio:.1f} times as much timed work). "
        f"All neural fits/monitoring took {neural_seconds/60:.2f} minutes; "
        f"logistic tuning took {r['logistic_seconds_including_tuning']:.2f} seconds. "
        "These timings depend on hardware and do not include every notebook operation. "
        "The energy table assumes power levels; electricity and emissions were not measured. "
        "Added complexity should be justified by quality, not by model size alone.",
        f"**What explanations establish.** The {len(shap_diagnostics)} selected word explanations "
        "help a reviewer challenge a suggestion by seeing which title words raised or lowered its score. "

        "These narrow checks concern calculation consistency and sampling variation, not causal truth or fairness. "

    return '\n\n'.join(text)

8. Export and reload deployment graphs¶

The function below converts the models trained in this notebook to PyTorch .pt2 graphs. It reloads only files it has just written, then checks logits and predicted classes at batch sizes 1, 2, the parity sample size, and 512. Preprocessing, labels and metadata are saved for future use, but this notebook never depends on a previous export.

The PyTorch export documentation describes this format. This is a local CPU demonstration requiring Python/PyTorch and fitted text preprocessing; it is not a hosted service or a hardware-compiled executable.

Why export with parity checks? A saved graph plus the fitted preprocessing, vocabulary, label order and manifest packages the current model consistently for later use. Reloading freshly written graphs avoids relying on earlier artifacts. Batch sizes 1, 2, a diverse parity sample and the 512 limit test practical batch shape behavior; logits and classes must match the in-memory model within stated numerical tolerances. Passing establishes fidelity for these sampled inputs, not semantic quality or readiness for a public service. Serialized preprocessing should be loaded only from trusted project outputs.

In [26]:
def export_current_models(models, vectorizer, vocabulary, prepared_frame, results, destination):
    destination.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    texts = prepared_frame.groupby(['split', 'label'], sort=True).head(4).text.tolist()
    texts += ['riqualificazione energetica scuola comunità', 'realizzazione nuovo ospedale comunità',
              'servizi digitali comunità ' * 40]
    manifest = {'format': 'torch.export ExportedProgram (.pt2)', 'torch_version': str(torch.__version__),
                'classes': results['classes'], 'sequence_length': results['sequence_length'],
                'max_batch_size': 512, 'models': {}}
    loaded = {}
    for kind, model in models.items():
        model.eval()
        features = (torch.from_numpy(vectorizer.transform(texts).toarray()) if kind == 'MLP'
                    else torch.from_numpy(encode(texts, vocabulary, results['sequence_length'])))
        batch = torch.export.Dim('batch', min=1, max=512)
        graph = torch.export.export(model, (features[:2],), dynamic_shapes={'x': {0: batch}})
        path = destination / f'{kind.lower()}.pt2'
        torch.export.save(graph, path)
        restored = torch.export.load(path).module()
        max_error = 0.0
        sizes = [1, 2, len(texts), 512]
        with torch.inference_mode():
            for size in sizes:
                x = features[torch.arange(size) % len(features)]
                original, deployed = model(x), restored(x)
                torch.testing.assert_close(original, deployed, atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-5)
                assert torch.equal(original.argmax(1), deployed.argmax(1))
                max_error = max(max_error, (original - deployed).abs().max().item())
        loaded[kind] = restored
        manifest['models'][kind] = {'file': path.name, 'selected_run': results['selected'][kind],
                                    'bytes': path.stat().st_size, 'max_absolute_logit_error': max_error,
                                    'parity_batch_sizes': sizes, 'distinct_parity_titles': len(texts)}
    with (destination / 'tfidf.pkl').open('wb') as handle:
        pickle.dump(vectorizer, handle)
    (destination / 'vocabulary.json').write_text(json.dumps(vocabulary, ensure_ascii=False))
    (destination / 'manifest.json').write_text(json.dumps(manifest, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False))
    return loaded, manifest

loaded_deployed, manifest = export_current_models(chosen_models, tfidf, vocab, prepared, r, OUT / 'deployment')
display(pd.DataFrame(manifest['models']).T)
print('Graph round-trip and predicted-class parity passed.')

8.1 Define inference using the reloaded graphs¶

All cleaning, encoding and prediction logic is executable below. No training class definitions are needed by the reloaded graph. Titles shorter than three cleaned words, empty/oversized batches, and inputs without any known features/tokens are rejected for review. Partial vocabulary shift and confidently wrong predictions remain possible; this is not calibrated abstention.

Why these input rules? Reusing cleaning/encoding prevents training–inference mismatch. The one-to-512 batch limit matches the exported graph's shape contract. Rejecting empty/short titles and inputs with no known features prevents obvious unsupported suggestions. Partial vocabulary shift, ambiguous titles and confidently wrong results remain possible, so these checks are not a calibrated abstention policy. Explicitly naming the output uncalibrated_probability makes the score's limitation visible to downstream users.

In [27]:
def classify_exported(titles, kind='MLP'):
    if kind not in loaded_deployed:
        raise ValueError('Model must be MLP or CNN')
    if not titles or len(titles) > 512:
        raise ValueError('Supply between 1 and 512 titles')
    cleaned = [clean_title(title) for title in titles]
    if any(len(title.split()) < 3 for title in cleaned):
        raise ValueError('Each title needs at least three meaningful words after cleaning')
    if kind == 'MLP':
        features = tfidf.transform(cleaned)
        if np.any(np.asarray(features.getnnz(axis=1)) == 0):
            raise ValueError('No known TF-IDF features; human review required')
        x = torch.from_numpy(features.toarray().astype(np.float32))
    else:
        features = encode(cleaned, vocab, r['sequence_length'])
        if np.any(~(features > 1).any(axis=1)):
            raise ValueError('No known tokens; human review required')
        x = torch.from_numpy(features)
    with torch.inference_mode():
        probabilities = loaded_deployed[kind](x).softmax(1).numpy()
    return [{'title': title, 'model': kind,
             'predicted_theme': classes[int(p.argmax())],
             'uncalibrated_probability': float(p.max())}
            for title, p in zip(titles, probabilities)]

8.2 Demonstrate deployment and check invalid inputs¶

These predictions come from the serialized-and-reloaded graphs. They are exploratory suggestions for human review, never funding decisions.

How to read the examples. These are demonstrations without independently reviewed correct labels. Agreement on a hospital title shows consistent model behavior; disagreement on the school/energy title illustrates multiple plausible activities and why a suggestion cannot replace a recorded category. A high score expresses the model's preference among its eight themes, not certainty about actual purpose. Invalid-input checks show that the implemented interface enforces its contract; they do not guarantee rejection of every unfamiliar or risky input.

In [28]:

        try:
            classify_exported(invalid, kind)
        except ValueError:
            pass
        else:
            raise AssertionError(f'Invalid input was accepted by {kind}')

9. Limitations, fairness, ethics, and design decisions¶

Limits and uncertainty. Programme themes are weak labels: a project title can describe an activity different from its programme category. No independent annotation was completed. The proposal's hypothesis about human-reviewed purposes therefore remains untested, and the 0.80 macro-F1 target is a goal, not a result. Group-held-out evaluation is harder and more realistic for unfamiliar measures than random row splitting. Only one split/seed is available; few test groups and vocabulary shift limit generalization. The paired bootstrap intervals are exploratory. Future snapshots, other languages, and excluded themes require new validation. Funding and payment analyses were not performed.

Fairness shaped evaluation and input choices. Large themes and standard administrative language could dominate learning, while small programmes, unusual wording, and under-resourced organizations could be misclassified more often. Macro-F1, class-weighted loss, per-class recall/F1, group isolation, and a minimum independent-group requirement make disparities more visible. Excluding low-support categories also removes their coverage; it does not make them unimportant. Dropping identifiers reduces shortcuts but does not eliminate bias or geographic proxies in titles. No protected-attribute or regional fairness audit was conducted, and class-level disparities cannot establish demographic fairness. Before public use, independently review labels across themes, territories, organization types and title lengths; measure errors/coverage with sample counts and uncertainty, and retain an unknown category.

Ethics shaped the intended use. Predictions are suggestions for a human reviewer, never evidence to award/deny funding, rank territorial performance, allege misconduct, or replace the recorded programme label. Confident errors shown above motivate retaining the original text/category and documenting uncertainty. The demo rejects malformed and entirely unknown inputs; a validated calibration/abstention policy is still needed. Public titles may contain personal names or addresses: identifier cleaning is not anonymization, so review examples before publication and avoid logging raw new-user titles unnecessarily. Source attribution and licence verification remain necessary before redistribution. Only local input files are used; no project text is sent to an external inference service.

Energy shaped the compute budget. Compact models, CPU execution, four threads, sparse TF–IDF batches, 80-token sequences, bounded vocabulary, two regularization choices, and early stopping limit compute. Opening this executed notebook permits inspecting saved outputs without new computation; Run All deliberately retrains from raw data. Each rerun incurs another training cost. The CNN's representation learning should justify its extra measured cost before expanding the search or adopting a larger model. Runtime is measured; electricity and emissions are not. The next cell gives transparent sensitivity scenarios rather than claiming measured energy savings.

10. Interpretation and next steps¶

The executed summary below is calculated from this run, so rerunning training cannot leave stale numerical conclusions. Further work should prioritize independently reviewed labels, more independent groups, repeated seeds, calibration and abstention, and a territory/organization audit before expanding deployment.
